concepts.def: Total momentum stays the same in a closed system

walkthroughs.body_html:
p = m × v

A 1500 kg car at 20 m/s has momentum 30 000 kg·m/s. That's a lot of oomph. 🚗

Momentum is a vector — direction matters.

A force acting over time changes momentum. F × t = Δp (impulse).

Rearrange: F = Δp ÷ t. That's Newton's 2nd law in full.

Crumple zones and airbags increase t in a crash, so F on the passenger is smaller. Safer! 🛡️

In a closed system: total momentum before = total momentum after.

A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick. Before: 6 kg·m/s. After: 3 kg × v. So v = 2 m/s.

Useful for collisions, explosions, and recoil.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of momentum?
A crumple zone reduces injury by:
If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.

mcqs.q: Does Hooke's law apply to a spring for any amount of stretching?
options: Yes — Hooke's law applies to any spring at any extension.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
No — it only holds up to the limit of proportionality; beyond that the relationship between force and extension is no longer linear.
